content.title: About
content.content: Hard candy is a sweet treat made from sugar, glucose syrup, flavorings, and sometimes colorants. When heated, the sugar crystallizes, forming a glossy, solid shell that slowly melts in the mouth, releasing aroma and taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hard candies appeared in Europe in the 19th century with the advent of the caramelization process.
Hard candies are often called “lollipops,” although the term can also refer to softer varieties.
There are over 100,000 flavors and aromas for hard candy, ranging from classic fruit to exotic and spicy.
The solid surface allows edible graphics and lettering to be printed with specialized equipment.
In some countries, traditional hard candies are shaped into small round “pastilles.”

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The sugar in candy is rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate boost of glucose to the bloodstream.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Sweet taste stimulates serotonin production, which can temporarily improve mood.

items.title: Contains trace minerals
items.content: Depending on added ingredients, candies may provide small amounts of calcium, iron, or magnesium.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption can contribute to weight gain, tooth decay, and metabolic disturbances.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some candies contain nuts, dairy, or gluten, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: The hard texture can pose a risk for young children; supervision is recommended.

items.title: Artificial colorants
items.content: Certain additives may cause hyperactivity or allergic responses in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hard candies are typically enjoyed one at a time, allowing them to slowly dissolve in the mouth. They can also be used as dessert decorations, added to baked goods, or given as small gifts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store candies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. High humidity can cause them to become sticky.

content.title: About
content.content: Fontina is a semi‑hard Italian cheese made from cow’s milk, originating in the Aosta Valley. It has a mild nutty flavor with a subtle sweetness and a buttery texture that melts smoothly when heated. The cheese is commonly used in hot dishes, gratins, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese is named after the town of Fontina in the Aosta Valley, where it has been traditionally produced.
Traditional Fontina is aged 3–6 months, during which a golden‑brown rind develops.
It is often called the “Italian Gruyère” because of its meltability and flavor profile.
Fontina is a key ingredient in classic fondue and is frequently used on pizza for a creamy melt.
The cheese holds a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) status in the European Union.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Fontina provides a good amount of calcium, which supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The cheese supplies high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B2 and B12 that aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Fontina includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that may benefit cardiovascular health.

items.title: Probiotic properties
items.content: As a fermented product, it can contribute to a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming the cheese.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Fontina contains a notable amount of salt, so individuals with hypertension should monitor portions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to casein.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The cheese is calorie‑dense, so it should be eaten in moderation as part of a balanced diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fontina works well grated over pasta, in casseroles, risotto, and salads. It can be cubed for hot sandwiches, melted in fondue, or enjoyed sliced on its own. The cheese melts beautifully, making it a popular choice for pizza and gratin dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Fontina in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage, it can be frozen, though texture may change. Discard any cheese that shows mold or off‑odors.

chicken-thigh-grilled-with-sauce-skin-ea.title: Chicken thigh, grilled with sauce, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is the dark meat from the upper part of a bird's leg. When grilled with sauce and the skin left on, the skin becomes crispy while the meat stays juicy. This dish is popular in many world cuisines and is often served as a main course or in salads and sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thighs contain more iron and zinc than breast meat due to richer blood supply.
Leaving the skin on during grilling adds flavor, texture, and beneficial fatty acids.
Marinades based on soy sauce, honey, or spices enhance aroma and help retain moisture.
In traditional American barbecue, “smoked thigh” is a common menu item served with a tangy sauce.
When grilled correctly, the skin can become crisp without burning if not overcooked.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamin B6, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals aid immune function and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Beneficial fats in the skin
items.content: The skin supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can support heart health when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Thighs with skin are more calorie‑dense than breast meat, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: The skin adds saturated fat, which in excess may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper cooking can leave bacteria such as Salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may have allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the thighs hot, sliced, in salads, tacos, sandwiches, or as a standalone dish with vegetable sides. The skin can be eaten for crunch or removed for a leaner option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh chicken thighs keep in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen thighs last up to 9 months. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge before cooking, and store cooked leftovers in an airtight container for no more than 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Pinto beans are dried beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) widely used in North and South American cuisines. They have a light‑brown color with speckles and a mild, slightly nutty flavor. Dried beans require soaking and cooking before they can be added to soups, stews, salads, or side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pinto beans are among the most consumed bean varieties in Mexico and the United States.
The name “pinto” comes from the Spanish word for “painted,” referring to the speckled appearance of the beans.
When kept dry and cool, dried beans can be stored for up to a year.
Pinto beans are a good source of complex carbohydrates, providing sustained energy.
They are traditionally used to make “refried beans,” a staple in Mexican cooking.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of dried pinto beans provides about 21 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Source of iron and magnesium
items.content: Pinto beans contain iron for oxygen transport and magnesium for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: These beans contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Contain antioxidants
items.content: Phytochemicals such as polyphenols help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals if consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals; thorough soaking and rinsing can help.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to beans, experiencing skin or digestive reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak pinto beans in water for at least 6–8 hours, drain, and then simmer for 1–1.5 hours until tender. Use them in soups, chili, salads, mash them for spreads, or incorporate into vegetarian patties. For a richer flavor, you can briefly sauté the cooked beans.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried pinto beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored, they keep their quality for up to 12 months. Discard beans that develop a moldy odor or show signs of moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Pudding is a smooth dessert made from milk, cream and thickeners, often flavored with varieties other than chocolate. The range includes vanilla, caramel, berry, coffee and coconut options. Pudding is served chilled, frequently topped with fruit, nuts or sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pudding has ancient roots: early recipes appear in Roman cuisine.
Unlike jelly, pudding thickens with starch, gelatin or egg yolk.
In Japan, “mochi‑puddings” incorporate glutinous rice flour for a chewy texture.
Vegan versions are made with plant milk and agar‑agar.
Pudding is often used as a base for cakes and dessert parfaits.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy base provides calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Depending on the flavor, pudding can contain B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Easily digestible protein
items.content: Egg yolk or milk adds a modest amount of complete protein.

items.title: Probiotic content
items.content: When yogurt or kefir is used, pudding can help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low‑sugar options
items.content: Sugar can be replaced with stevia or erythritol, lowering the glycemic impact.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or casein allergy should choose plant‑based versions.

items.title: High sugar content in traditional recipes
items.content: Excess sugar may contribute to weight gain and increase cavity risk.

items.title: Thickener additives
items.content: Some artificial thickeners can cause intolerance in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Pudding made with cream can be calorie‑rich; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pudding chilled in individual glasses or bowls, garnished with berries, fruit sauces, nuts, honey or sprinkles. It can be layered in cakes, used as a filling for pastries, or enjoyed as a light evening dessert.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared pudding in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized containers; thaw in the fridge before serving and gently stir if needed.

content.title: About
content.content: Wild rice (Zizania aquatica) is a grain harvested from aquatic grasses native to North America. This product is fully cooked and enriched with added plant fat, making it more caloric and flavorful. It has a nutty taste, slightly chewy texture, and can be used as a side dish or a base for various meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wild rice is not a true rice; it belongs to the grass family and is more closely related to corn.
Native American tribes traditionally harvested wild rice for food and ceremonial purposes.
Compared with regular rice, wild rice contains more protein and fiber.
Cooking with added fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin E.
Wild rice is often featured in salads, soups, and stuffed vegetable dishes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Wild rice provides about 14 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Source of magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are essential for bone health and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: The added plant fats supply vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Wild rice raises blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for glucose control.

items.title: Allergy to added fats
items.content: Some individuals may react to the oils used in the product.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Added fat increases the energy density, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Wild rice can accumulate arsenic from soil; choose reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked wild rice with fat can be served as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable dishes, mixed into salads, soups, and casseroles, or used in vegetarian recipes as a substitute for rice or quinoa.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the product in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it refrigerated to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Cola is a carbonated soft drink with a sweet flavor, made from caramelized sugar, flavorings, caffeine and carbon dioxide. It is commonly enjoyed as a refreshing beverage in restaurants, cafés, and at home.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial cola recipe was created in 1886 by John Pemberton.
The dark color comes from caramel, not from the cola plant.
Cola typically contains 30–40 mg of caffeine per 330 ml.
Various countries produce low‑sugar and diet versions without added sugar.
Glass bottles preserve the taste longer than plastic containers.

items.title: Boosts energy
items.content: Caffeine in cola can temporarily increase alertness and concentration.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like any beverage, cola contributes to overall fluid intake when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Caramel flavoring provides small amounts of polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Regular consumption can lead to weight gain and dental caries.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Excessive caffeine may cause anxiety, insomnia, and rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic pH can irritate the stomach lining and promote reflux.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of certain stimulants and reduce the efficacy of some sedatives.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Cola is usually served chilled in a glass with ice. It can be used in cocktails, as a base for marinades, or in recipes that call for a sweet carbonated liquid.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cola in a cool, dark place, keeping the bottle or can sealed. After opening, consume within a few days to retain carbonation.
